gloss: A garment for the upper body, usually with a collar and buttons down the front.
examples: He ironed a white *shirt* for the interview.
All my *shirts* are still in the dryer.
You've got ketchup on your *shirt*.

gloss: A loose shirt worn by women.
examples: She wore a silk *blouse* under her blazer.
The store had *blouses* on sale for twenty bucks.
That *blouse* looks great with those pants.
contrast: Americans end it with an s sound, rhyming with house; the British end it with a z sound.

gloss: A light cotton shirt with short sleeves and no collar.
examples: He sleeps in an old *t-shirt* and shorts.
They handed out free *t-shirts* at the race.
Can you grab me a clean *t-shirt*?

gloss: A knitted garment worn on the upper body for warmth.
examples: Bring a *sweater* — it gets cold at night.
She knits *sweaters* for her grandkids.
My *sweater* shrank in the wash.
contrast: The ea sounds like the e in bed, not like the ea in sweet. What Americans call a sweater the British usually call a jumper.

gloss: A loose heavy cotton top with long sleeves, worn casually.
examples: He threw on a *sweatshirt* and went for a run.
The team sells *sweatshirts* at every home game.
Her *sweatshirt* had the college logo across the front.

gloss: A sweatshirt with a hood.
examples: He pulled his *hoodie* up when it started raining.
Half the class showed up in *hoodies*.
That gray *hoodie* is my favorite thing to wear.

gloss: A sweater that you put on over your head, with no opening at the front.
examples: She bought a wool *pullover* for the trip.
The store had *pullovers* in three colors.
This *pullover* is a little tight in the shoulders.

gloss: A knitted sweater that opens down the front and fastens with buttons.
examples: He wore a gray *cardigan* over his shirt.
She has *cardigans* in every color.
Button up your *cardigan* — it's chilly in here.

gloss: A short coat worn on the upper body.
examples: Grab your *jacket*, it's windy out.
He keeps his keys in his *jacket* pocket.
Both *jackets* were left on the back of the chair.

gloss: A long outer garment worn over other clothes for warmth.
examples: She hung her *coat* by the door.
The *coats* are in the front closet.
You'll need a heavier *coat* in Chicago.

gloss: A long heavy coat worn over a suit or other clothes in cold weather.
examples: He buttoned his *overcoat* against the wind.
That old wool *overcoat* still fits him.
Most of the men wore dark *overcoats*.

gloss: A waterproof coat that keeps you dry in wet weather.
examples: Take a *raincoat* — it's supposed to pour.
Her yellow *raincoat* was easy to spot in the crowd.
The kids left their *raincoats* at school again.

gloss: A long belted raincoat with a wide collar.
examples: He showed up in a tan *trench coat*.
That *trench coat* has been in style for decades.
The rack by the door was full of *trench coats*.

gloss: A light jacket that keeps out the wind.
examples: She zipped up her *windbreaker* at the top of the hill.
A thin *windbreaker* is enough for this weather.
The whole team wore matching *windbreakers*.

gloss: A heavy hooded winter coat.
examples: You need a real *parka* for a winter like this.
He shook the snow off his *parka* in the hallway.
The store sold out of *parkas* by November.

gloss: A sleeveless garment worn over a shirt, often as part of a suit.
examples: He wore a three-piece suit with a matching *vest*.
The crew put on orange safety *vests*.
A down *vest* keeps your core warm without the bulk.
contrast: An American vest is a British waistcoat; a British vest is what Americans call an undershirt.

gloss: A tailored jacket worn as part of an outfit but not with matching pants.
examples: She threw a *blazer* on over her t-shirt.
He owns two navy *blazers* and wears them constantly.
A *blazer* and jeans is fine for this office.

gloss: A set of matching jacket and pants or skirt worn together.
examples: He wore a dark gray *suit* to the wedding.
Her *suits* are all custom made.
You don't need a *suit* for this interview.
contrast: Say SOOT in American English, and don't confuse it with suite /swiːt/, a set of rooms.

gloss: A formal black suit worn by men at evening events.
examples: He rented a *tuxedo* for the wedding.
The waiters all wore *tuxedos*.
His *tuxedo* still had the tag on the sleeve.
contrast: Americans say tuxedo, or tux for short; the British say dinner jacket.

gloss: A set of clothes worn by all the members of a school, team, or organization.
examples: The nurses on that floor wear blue *uniforms*.
He still has his old army *uniform* in a box.
Her school makes everyone wear a *uniform*.

gloss: A one-piece garment for women that covers the body and part of the legs.
examples: She bought a red *dress* for the party.
All the bridesmaids wore the same *dress*.
These *dresses* are on the clearance rack.

gloss: A long formal dress, or a loose robe worn for a special purpose.
examples: She wore a floor-length *gown* to the ceremony.
The graduates picked up their caps and *gowns* on Friday.
The nurse handed him a hospital *gown* and left.

gloss: A garment that hangs from the waist and covers part of the legs.
examples: She wore a black *skirt* and a white blouse.
That *skirt* is too short for the office.
Most of her *skirts* come down to the knee.

gloss: A sleeveless shirt with wide shoulder straps.
examples: It was too hot for anything but a *tank top*.
He works out in a *tank top* and shorts.
She packed three *tank tops* for the beach.

gloss: A sweater or shirt with a high collar that folds over and covers the neck.
examples: He wore a black *turtleneck* under his jacket.
*Turtlenecks* are back in style this year.
That *turtleneck* looks itchy.
contrast: Americans say turtleneck; the British say polo neck.

gloss: A shirt worn by a member of a sports team, usually with a number on the back.
examples: He got the goalie to sign his *jersey*.
The team is wearing their away *jerseys* tonight.
Her *jersey* had her last name across the shoulders.

gloss: A one-piece garment with a top and pants joined together.
examples: She wore a black *jumpsuit* to the party.
The mechanics work in heavy canvas *jumpsuits*.
That *jumpsuit* is surprisingly comfortable.

gloss: A loose garment worn over other clothes or for lounging at home.
examples: He shuffled into the kitchen in his *robe*.
The hotel leaves *robes* hanging in the closet.
Her *robe* was on the hook behind the bathroom door.

gloss: A loose robe worn before or after bathing.
examples: She threw on a *bathrobe* and answered the door.
The kids ran around in their *bathrobes* after the pool.
My *bathrobe* is still damp from this morning.

gloss: A loose dress-like garment that a woman or girl sleeps in.
examples: She was still in her *nightgown* at noon.
Grandma packed two *nightgowns* for the trip.
The little girl's *nightgown* had stars all over it.

gloss: A long loose outer garment with no sleeves, worn over the shoulders.
examples: The actor swept onstage in a black *cloak*.
Travelers once wore heavy *cloaks* against the cold.
His *cloak* was fastened at the throat with a pin.

gloss: A short sleeveless garment that hangs from the shoulders down the back.
examples: The kid wore a superhero *cape* to school.
The barber tied a *cape* around my neck.
*Capes* were everywhere at the costume party.

gloss: A loose outer garment made of one piece of cloth with a hole for the head.
examples: They handed out plastic *ponchos* at the gate.
She pulled a *poncho* on over her backpack.
A *poncho* beats an umbrella in wind like that.

gloss: A large piece of cloth worn over the shoulders or head.
examples: She wrapped a wool *shawl* around her shoulders.
The vendors were selling hand-knit *shawls*.
Take a *shawl* — the church is always drafty.

gloss: A garment tied over the front of your clothes to keep them clean while you cook or work.
examples: He tied on an *apron* before he started cooking.
The bakery hands out *aprons* to new hires.
Her *apron* was covered in flour.
contrast: The first syllable rhymes with ape, not with app.

gloss: A garment worn for swimming.
examples: Don't forget your *swimsuit*.
Her *swimsuit* was still wet from yesterday.
The stores put *swimsuits* out in February.

gloss: A two-piece swimsuit for women.
examples: She wore a red *bikini* to the beach.
The shop had *bikinis* hanging right by the door.
That *bikini* was way more expensive than it looked.

gloss: A set of clothes worn to look like someone or something else, as in a play or at a party.
examples: His Halloween *costume* was a giant hot dog.
The theater keeps its *costumes* in the basement.
She sewed the whole *costume* herself.
contrast: A false friend: Russian костюм in the everyday sense is a suit. An English costume is theatrical or for a party.

gloss: A set of clothes worn together.
examples: She picked out her *outfit* the night before.
He wore the same *outfit* three days in a row.
Those *outfits* are way too formal for a picnic.

gloss: A single piece of clothing.
examples: Wash this *garment* in cold water only.
The factory turns out about a thousand *garments* a day.
Every *garment* in the store is handmade.

gloss: All the clothes a person owns, or a tall closet for hanging clothes.
examples: She updated her whole *wardrobe* for the new job.
His *wardrobe* is basically jeans and t-shirts.
They built *wardrobes* into both bedrooms.

gloss: Clothing, especially of a particular kind or for a particular occasion.
examples: The invitation said formal *attire*.
Business *attire* is required in the main dining room.
He showed up in hiking *attire* and nobody minded.
contrast: Uncountable — say formal attire or a piece of attire, never an attire or attires.

gloss: Clothing, especially as sold in stores.
examples: Women's *apparel* is on the second floor.
They sell athletic *apparel* online.
Sales of winter *apparel* were up again this year.
contrast: Uncountable — say an item of apparel, never an apparel or apparels.

gloss: Clothing worn outdoors over your other clothes.
examples: Leave your *outerwear* in the hall closet.
The shop specializes in winter *outerwear*.
Heavy *outerwear* is a must up north.
contrast: Uncountable — never outerwears.

gloss: Clothing worn next to the skin under your other clothes.
examples: He packed a week's worth of *underwear*.
Put your dirty *underwear* in the hamper.
The store sells *underwear* three pairs to a pack.
contrast: Uncountable, even though бельё feels countable — say some underwear or a pair of underwear, never an underwear or underwears.

gloss: A light shirt worn under another shirt, next to the skin.
examples: He wears a white *undershirt* under his dress shirt.
She bought him a pack of *undershirts*.
You can see the *undershirt* through that fabric.
contrast: An American undershirt is a British vest.

gloss: An undergarment that supports a woman's breasts.
examples: She bought two *bras* at the department store.
The *bra* straps kept slipping off her shoulders.
A sports *bra* is much more comfortable for running.

gloss: A thick pad of cloth or paper fastened around a baby's bottom.
examples: Somebody in here needs a clean *diaper*.
We go through about ten *diapers* a day.
He learned to change a *diaper* fast.
contrast: Americans say diaper; the British say nappy.

gloss: A piece of cloth or plastic tied under a child's chin to keep food off their clothes.
examples: Put a *bib* on him before you feed him.
All the *bibs* are in the wash.
Her *bib* was covered in spaghetti sauce.

gloss: A covering for the foot with a firm sole, not reaching above the ankle.
examples: Take your *shoes* off at the door.
He tied his *shoe* and kept running.
These *shoes* are killing my feet.

gloss: A heavy shoe that covers the ankle and sometimes part of the leg.
examples: She pulled on her rain *boots*.
One *boot* is still sitting by the back door.
You'll want hiking *boots* on that trail.
contrast: In Britain the boot is also the trunk of a car.

gloss: A light open shoe held on the foot by straps.
examples: He wore *sandals* all summer.
One *sandal* broke on the second day of the trip.
Those *sandals* are not made for hiking.

gloss: A soft shoe with a rubber sole, worn for sports or casual wear.
examples: He bought a new pair of *sneakers*.
My *sneakers* are completely soaked.
White *sneakers* go with almost anything.
contrast: Americans say sneakers; the British say trainers.

gloss: A soft comfortable shoe worn indoors.
examples: He shuffled downstairs in his *slippers*.
Keep a pair of *slippers* by the bed.
One *slipper* has gone missing again.

gloss: A flat leather shoe with no laces that you slip onto your foot.
examples: He wore brown *loafers* with khakis.
That *loafer* has a hole worn through the sole.
*Loafers* are a lot easier than lacing up boots.

gloss: A light open sandal held on by a strap between the toes.
examples: She lives in *flip-flops* all summer.
One *flip-flop* floated off across the pool.
You can't wear *flip-flops* on the job site.

gloss: A soft covering for the foot worn inside a shoe.
examples: He can never find two matching *socks*.
There's a hole in my *sock*.
Put on some wool *socks* if your feet are cold.

gloss: A close-fitting covering for the foot and leg, usually of thin material.
examples: She snagged her *stocking* on the chair.
The dancers wore black *stockings*.
The kids hung their *stockings* by the fireplace.

gloss: The raised part at the back of a shoe under the back of the foot.
examples: The *heel* on my boot is worn down.
She can't run in those *heels*.
He broke a *heel* on the cobblestones.
contrast: Sounds exactly like heal, the verb meaning to get better.

gloss: The flat bottom part of a shoe that touches the ground.
examples: The *sole* of my sneaker is coming loose.
These boots have thick rubber *soles*.
He glued the *sole* back on and it held.
contrast: Sounds exactly like soul; the same spelling is also a flat fish.

gloss: A cord used to tie a shoe.
examples: Tie your *shoelaces* before you trip.
One *shoelace* snapped this morning.
He bought new *shoelaces* for his work boots.

gloss: Shoes, boots, and other coverings for the feet.
examples: Closed-toe *footwear* is required in the lab.
The store carries *footwear* for the whole family.
Proper *footwear* makes a long walk much easier.
contrast: Uncountable — never a footwear or footwears; say a pair of shoes instead.

gloss: A covering for the head, often with a brim.
examples: Wear a *hat* — the sun is brutal today.
He collects old baseball *hats*.
Her *hat* blew off halfway down the block.

gloss: A soft flat hat, usually with a stiff curved brim at the front.
examples: He wore a baseball *cap* backwards.
The team handed out free *caps* at the gate.
Take your *cap* off at the table.

gloss: A close-fitting knitted hat worn in cold weather.
examples: He pulled a *beanie* down over his ears.
She knits *beanies* for everyone every winter.
My *beanie* is in the pocket of my coat.

gloss: A hard hat that protects the head.
examples: Always wear a *helmet* when you ride.
The workers left their *helmets* in the truck.
His *helmet* probably saved his life in that crash.

gloss: The part of a coat or sweatshirt that covers the head.
examples: He put his *hood* up when it started to drizzle.
The jacket has a *hood* that zips off.
Both coats have fur-lined *hoods*.
contrast: The vowel is short, like book, not like food. In American English the hood is also the front cover over a car engine.

gloss: A piece of thin cloth worn over the face or head.
examples: The bride lifted her *veil*.
The shop sells *veils* in three different lengths.
Her *veil* caught on the church door.
contrast: Sounds exactly like vale, a valley.

gloss: A soft round flat hat with no brim.
examples: She wore a red *beret* to the gallery.
The soldiers wore green *berets*.
His *beret* sat at an angle over one ear.
contrast: The final t is silent, and Americans stress the second syllable: buh-RAY.

gloss: A stiff piece at the front of a cap or helmet that shades or protects the eyes.
examples: He flipped down the *visor* on his helmet.
She wore a tennis *visor* on the court.
The *visors* on those old caps are all cracked.

gloss: A large colored square of cloth worn around the head or neck.
examples: He tied a *bandana* around his forehead.
She keeps a *bandana* in her back pocket.
The stand sold *bandanas* in every color.

gloss: A head covering made by winding a long piece of cloth around the head.
examples: He wrapped a white *turban* around his head.
The men in the photograph are wearing *turbans*.
His *turban* matched the color of his jacket.

gloss: A strip of material worn around the head.
examples: She pushed her hair back with a *headband*.
The runners all wore sweat *headbands*.
My *headband* keeps sliding off.

gloss: The part of a garment that covers the arm.
examples: He rolled up his *sleeves* and got to work.
There's a stain on your left *sleeve*.
The dress has long *sleeves* and a high collar.

gloss: The band of material around the neck of a shirt or coat.
examples: He turned up his *collar* against the wind.
The *collar* on this shirt is fraying.
Both shirts have button-down *collars*.
contrast: Say KAH-lur; it is not the same word as color, KUH-lur.

gloss: The band of material at the end of a sleeve, or the turned-up bottom of a pant leg.
examples: He unbuttoned his *cuffs* and rolled up his sleeves.
There was ink all over his *cuff*.
The tailor let out the *cuffs* on the pants.

gloss: A small bag sewn into a garment for carrying things.
examples: He shoved his hands in his *pockets*.
My phone is in my back *pocket*.
This coat has *pockets* on the inside too.

gloss: The bottom edge of a garment, folded over and sewn.
examples: The *hem* of her skirt came loose.
He let the *hem* down on the pants.
Both dresses need new *hems*.

gloss: The line where two pieces of cloth are sewn together.
examples: The *seam* split right down the side.
Check the *seams* before you buy it.
She sewed the *seam* back up by hand.
contrast: Sounds exactly like seem, the verb.

gloss: A layer of material sewn inside a garment.
examples: The jacket has a silk *lining*.
The *lining* of my coat is torn at the shoulder.
Winter boots with fleece *linings* are worth the money.

gloss: The folded flap of cloth on the front of a jacket, joined to the collar.
examples: He pinned the badge to his *lapel*.
The *lapels* on that suit are too wide.
She brushed a piece of lint off his *lapel*.
contrast: Stress the second syllable: luh-PEL, not LAY-pel.

gloss: A narrow strip of material used to fasten or carry something.
examples: One *strap* on her sandal broke.
Tighten the *straps* on your backpack.
The *strap* kept sliding off her shoulder.

gloss: The band of material at the top of pants or a skirt that fits around the waist.
examples: The *waistband* on these jeans is too tight.
He tucked his shirt in behind the *waistband*.
The *waistbands* are elastic, so one size fits most.
contrast: Waist sounds exactly like waste.

gloss: The shape of the opening at the neck of a garment.
examples: The dress has a low *neckline*.
She usually prefers a higher *neckline*.
Both tops have the same round *neckline*.

gloss: A fold pressed or sewn into cloth.
examples: Her skirt has *pleats* all the way around.
He ironed the *pleat* back into his slacks.
The *pleats* fell out after one wash.

gloss: One loop of thread made by a needle when sewing.
examples: A few *stitches* came out along the hem.
She put in one more *stitch* and cut the thread.
The *stitches* on this bag are already coming apart.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A thin strand of cotton or other material used for sewing.
examples: Do you have any black *thread*?
He pulled a loose *thread* off his sleeve.
She keeps a dozen colors of *thread* in that box.
contrast: The ea sounds like the e in red, not like the ee in reed.

gloss: A small piece of cloth sewn over a hole or onto a garment as a decoration.
examples: She sewed a *patch* over the hole in his jeans.
His jacket is covered in band *patches*.
The scouts get a *patch* for every skill they learn.

gloss: A small piece of material inside a garment giving its size and care instructions.
examples: The *label* says dry clean only.
He cut the itchy *label* out of his shirt.
Check the *labels* before you put anything in the dryer.

gloss: A small piece of card or plastic attached to a new garment showing the price or size.
examples: The *tag* is still on your sweater.
She checked the price *tag* and put it back.
Cut the *tags* off before you wear it.

gloss: The flat edge that sticks out around the bottom of a hat.
examples: He tipped the *brim* of his hat.
A wide *brim* keeps the sun off your face.
The rain ran off the *brims* of their hats.

gloss: A cord threaded through a garment that you pull to tighten it.
examples: He tightened the *drawstring* on his shorts.
The hood has a *drawstring* on each side.
Both *drawstrings* came out in the wash.

gloss: A small round fastener that fits through a hole to hold a garment closed.
examples: A *button* came off my shirt this morning.
She sewed the *button* back on in two minutes.
The coat has big wooden *buttons*.

gloss: The slit in a garment that a button fits through.
examples: The *buttonhole* has stretched out.
He slipped a flower into his *buttonhole*.
The *buttonholes* on this shirt are hand-sewn.

gloss: A metal fastener at the end of a belt or strap.
examples: His belt *buckle* was the size of a saucer.
The *buckle* on my sandal came loose.
Both straps have plastic *buckles*.

gloss: A fastener with two parts that press together to close a garment.
examples: The shirt closes with *snaps* instead of buttons.
One *snap* on the jacket is broken.
Baby clothes with *snaps* are so much easier.
contrast: Americans call it a snap; the British call it a press stud or a popper.

gloss: A small curved piece of metal used to fasten a garment or hang it up.
examples: The dress fastens with a *hook* at the back.
One of the *hooks* on the skirt is bent.
She hung her coat on the *hook* by the door.

gloss: A fastener that holds two parts together.
examples: The *clasp* on the cloak was solid silver.
She fumbled with the tiny *clasp* at the back of the dress.
Both *clasps* on the belt had rusted shut.

gloss: A thin piece of metal with a sharp point, used to hold cloth together.
examples: The tailor held the hem in place with *pins*.
Watch out — there's still a *pin* in that shirt.
She dropped a whole box of *pins* on the floor.

gloss: Anything used to hold a garment closed, such as a button, hook, or snap.
examples: The dress has a hidden *fastener* at the side.
All the *fasteners* on this jacket are plastic.
One *fastener* is missing from the cuff.
contrast: The t is silent: FAS-nur, like fasten, listen, and castle.

gloss: A strip of leather or cloth worn around the waist.
examples: He tightened his *belt* one more notch.
That dress comes with a matching *belt*.
His *belts* are all hanging on the closet door.

gloss: A small fastener used to hold together the cuffs of a dress shirt.
examples: He wore silver *cufflinks* to the wedding.
One *cufflink* rolled under the dresser.
His father's *cufflinks* still fit the shirt perfectly.

gloss: A covering for the hand with a separate part for each finger.
examples: Put your *gloves* on, it's freezing out there.
He lost a *glove* on the bus.
These *gloves* are too thin for skiing.
contrast: Rhymes with love, not with stove.

gloss: A hand covering with one section for the thumb and one for all the other fingers.
examples: The baby kept pulling off her *mittens*.
One *mitten* always goes missing by February.
Wool *mittens* are warmer than gloves.

gloss: A long narrow piece of cloth worn around the neck under a shirt collar.
examples: He loosened his *tie* on the way home.
She gave him a silk *tie* for his birthday.
All his *ties* hang on a rack in the closet.

gloss: A short tie fastened at the neck in the shape of a bow.
examples: He can never get a *bow tie* straight.
The waiters all wore black *bow ties*.
That *bow tie* is actually a clip-on.
contrast: Bow here rhymes with know, not with now.

gloss: A shaped piece of wire, wood, or plastic for hanging up clothes.
examples: Put your jacket on a *hanger*.
The closet is full of empty *hangers*.
That wire *hanger* left marks in the shoulders.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A fine open fabric with patterns of holes, or a cord for tying a shoe.
examples: Her dress had *lace* around the collar.
He pulled the *laces* tight and double-knotted them.
The tablecloth was trimmed with white *lace*.
contrast: The fabric is uncountable — some lace, never a lace; a shoe cord is countable — one lace, two laces.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Material made by weaving cotton, wool, or another fiber, or a piece of it used for cleaning.
examples: The coat is made of heavy wool *cloth*.
Wipe the counter with a damp *cloth*.
She keeps clean *cloths* under the sink.
contrast: The material is uncountable; a rag for cleaning is countable, plural cloths. Watch the sounds: cloth /klɔːθ/, clothe /kloʊð/, clothes /kloʊz/.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Cloth used for making clothes and other things.
examples: This *fabric* wrinkles if you look at it wrong.
The store sells *fabrics* by the yard.
Pick a *fabric* that breathes in the heat.

gloss: A soft white fiber made into cloth and thread.
examples: The shirt is a hundred percent *cotton*.
*Cotton* is a lot cooler than polyester in summer.
She only buys *cotton* sheets.

gloss: The soft hair of sheep, used to make cloth and yarn.
examples: The sweater is pure *wool*.
*Wool* keeps you warm even when it's damp.
She's allergic to *wool* and can't wear it.
contrast: Rhymes with full and pull, not with cool.

gloss: A fine soft cloth made from the threads produced by silkworms.
examples: That scarf is real *silk*.
*Silk* has to be washed by hand.
He wore a tie made of heavy *silk*.

gloss: Material made from animal skin, used for shoes, coats, and belts.
examples: The jacket is real *leather*.
*Leather* stretches out after you've worn it a while.
These boots are lined with soft *leather*.
contrast: The ea sounds like the e in bed, and the th is voiced, as in father.

gloss: A strong cotton cloth used to make jeans and jackets.
examples: The jacket is heavy *denim*.
*Denim* softens up after a few washes.
She wore a *denim* skirt and sneakers.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The thick soft hair covering an animal, used to make or line clothing.
examples: The hood is trimmed with *fur*.
She inherited her grandmother's *furs*.
Fake *fur* looks almost real these days.

gloss: Soft leather with a slightly rough, velvety surface.
examples: The boots are brown *suede*.
*Suede* stains the second it rains.
He bought a *suede* jacket in Italy.
contrast: One syllable, pronounced SWAYD; the ue is not a separate sound.

gloss: A light cloth made from flax, or household items such as sheets and towels.
examples: He wore a white *linen* shirt in the heat.
*Linen* wrinkles no matter what you do.
The hotel changes the *linen* every day.

gloss: A thick soft cloth with a short raised pile on one side.
examples: The dress was deep red *velvet*.
*Velvet* shows every fingerprint.
She lined the box with black *velvet*.

gloss: A synthetic material used to make clothes.
examples: The shirt is a cotton and *polyester* blend.
*Polyester* barely wrinkles, which is the whole point.
That jacket is cheap *polyester* and it feels like it.
